# Page 3^page=3
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservice architectural style • Before microservices • Monolithic systems • Applications delivered as single deployable software artifacts: UI, business, and database access logic packaged together into a single artifact deployed to an application server • “...the microservice architectural style is an approach to developing a single application as a suite of small services, each running in its own process and communicating with lightweight mechanisms, often an HTTP resource API” • Martin Fowler: https://martinfowler.com/articles/microservices.html SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 3

# Page 4^page=4
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservice architectural style • Microservices • Monolithic systems are decomposed into small specialized services and deal with a single bounded context in the target domain SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 4 Bounded context → single concern according to the application domain (single area of responsibility)

# Page 5^page=5
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservice architectural style • Successful stories • Netflix • Amazon • eBay • Spotify • … • [2010-2016] They all migrated from monolithic systems to microservices • Main goal: improve both process and product to support massive scale of operation (millions of users) SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 5

From monolithic architectures to microservices Load Balancer Monolithic App Account Component Catalog Component Recommendation Component Customer Service Component Database Gateway Account Component Account Component Recommendation Component Recommendation Component Recommendation Component Recommendation Component Catalog Component Catalog Component Catalog Component Customer Service Component SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 8

# Page 7^page=7
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: advantages (product) SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 9 • Enable fine-grained scaling strategies • In monolithic systems, selective replication is not possible, the entire system must be replicated as a whole • Microservices enable flexible deployment and selective replication • Reduce the scale of localized issues • Example: availability issues • [2008] Before migration to microservices, Netflix reported that a single minor syntax error in the codebase brought down the whole platform for many hours • Improved resilience • If a microservice fails the others can still work, possibly with a degraded functionality (until the failure is resolved)

# Page 8^page=8
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: advantages (product) SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 10 • Better reuse and composability • The functionality offered by a microservice can be used and reused in multiple contexts (e.g., authentication) • It is possible to compose multiple microservices in different ways to realize different workflows

# Page 9^page=9
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: advantages (process) SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 11 services data MVC deploy Multiple teams single artifact Each team has their own areas of responsibility with their own requirements and delivery demands All their work is synchronized into a single code base Multiple teams deploy deploy deploy deploy multiple artifacts Invokes all business logic as REST-based service calls The entire application has knowledge and access to all the data sources used within the application

# Page 10^page=10
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: advantages (process) SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 12 • Reduced teams synchronization overhead • Organizations have small development teams with well-defined areas of responsibility • Underlying technical implementation of the service is irrelevant because the applications always communicate through technology- neutral protocols (REST APIs) • Teams decide languages and technologies according to expertise and purpose (e.g., data analysis vs video streaming) • Teams can experiment with new technologies on a single microservice • Smaller codebase → easier debugging, cheaper maintenance

# Page 11^page=11
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Anatomy of a microservice SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 15 REST API exposes core operations of the service: - different types (HTTP verbs: GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE) - lightweight data serialization (JSON format) to send and receive data 3 main elements of a microservice Application (or business) logic implementation of core operations executed upon requests Data storage each microservice typically has its own local data (limited data sharing, no global DBs)

# Page 12^page=12
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Anatomy of a microservice (recap) SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 16 Common workflow of REST operations Once the data has been mapped, the microservice will execute the business logic. The logic may call operations exposed by other microservices. Once the microservice has identified the route it will map any parameters defined inside the route to arguments of the corresponding method The client receives the response from the microservice as JSON. The success/failure of the call is returned as HTTP status code A client makes a HTTP GET request to the Hello microservice The microservice will parse the HTTP request and map verb, URL, resource, and parameters to a method in the codebase Additional parameters can be passed through JSON in the HTTP body. These map to objects used by the method. JSON -> object mapping object -> JSON mapping Once the business logic is executed, the microservice will convert returned objects to JSON. 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 verb URL resource parameters Hello microservice

# Page 13^page=13
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: besides business logic SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 17 Resiliency patterns Routing patterns Routing patterns Loosely coupled How do I choose between synchronous and asynchronous modes? Communication patterns Secure How do I determine whether the service client calling a microservice is allowed to undertake certain actions? Security patterns

# Page 14^page=14
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: routing patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 21 • Execution environment has shared + not pre-allocated resources → • Physical location of running services is potentially unknown • Services need to be discovered • Service discovery must be • Highly available: cluster of nodes to avoid single point of failure (if a node becomes unavailable, other nodes in the cluster take over) • Load balanced: service invocations are spread across all the service instances • Resilient: if service discovery becomes (temporarily) unavailable, applications should still function and locate the services • Fault-tolerant: should monitor the health status of services and take action without human intervention

# Page 15^page=15
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: routing patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 22 • Service discovery architecture (1) — general concepts 0. When a service instance comes online it registers its location (IP/port) to one discovery service instance. Instances of the same service are registered under the same service ID. 1. A service location can be looked up by a logical name from the discovery nodes. Clients do not have direct knowledge of service locations. 2. Service discovery nodes share information (location/health) among each other. Propagation can use static lists, or P2P “gossip” protocols. 3. Service instances send periodic heartbeat (push mode) to service discovery. If an instance dies, the discovery layer removes its location. Dynamic set (instances are added/removed) Cluster of nodes Logical name Service ID IP Port /api/v1/serivicea ServiceA 172.18.32.100 172.18.32.100 172.18.32.101 8092 9092 9092 Client services

# Page 16^page=16
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: routing patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 24 • Service discovery architecture (2) – client-side cache and load balancing client machine 1. Client checks its local cache for the location of service instances. Client decides how to spread requests to instances (load balancing policy). Usually “round-robin.” 2. Client sends direct requests to service instances. 3. Periodic refresh of cached data by contacting the discovery engine. Client cache is eventually (but not always) consistent. Client services

# Page 17^page=17
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: routing patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 25 • Service discovery architecture with cache — possible issues • Does not ensure consistency of cached data → • When a client contacts a dead instance, the client invalidates the local cache and forces a refresh by contacting the service discovery engine.

# Page 18^page=18
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: resiliency patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 26 • “How do I make sure when there is a problem with a service, clients can avoid it before recovery?” • Service discovery provides some degree of resilience in the simple case in which a service instance dies (no heartbeat) • There are other subtle issues, for instance, remote resources could: • Throw errors (e.g., temporary bursts of exceptions) • Perform poorly (e.g., temporary slowdown) • Goal: allow clients to “fail fast” • Avoid useless resource consumption • Avoid ripple effects

# Page 19^page=19
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: resiliency patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 27 • Circuit breaker (CB) — Client-side resiliency pattern • CB acts as a proxy for a remote service • When a remote service is called, the CB monitors the call • Possible failures: • CB receives 5xx error • Call takes «too long» (CB kills the call) • «too many» failures → circuit breaker inhibits future calls Circuit breaker Client Service A Service B call/drop call after time t

# Page 20^page=20
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: resiliency patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 28 • Example — circuit breaker in action Network-Attached Storage (shared file system) Service A calls B to do some work Service B calls C Service A uses Data Manager A Service B has multiple instances, each one talks to Data Manager B Service C reads/writes data from NAS • Scenario • During the night operators change the config of NAS • The day after, reads to a particular disk subsystem start performing extremely slowly • Developers of Service B did not anticipate slowdowns occurring with calls to C • Service B writes into Data Manager B and gets data from Service C within the same transaction Data Manager A Data Manager B

# Page 21^page=21
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: resiliency patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 29 • Example — circuit breaker in action • What happens? (ripple effect) • C starts running slowly • Pending requests to C grow • Number of concurrent DB connections grow • Resources become exhausted because Service C never completes • Service A starts running out of resources because it calls B that is slow because of C Network-Attached Storage (shared file system) Service A calls B to do some work. Service B calls C. Service A uses Data Manager A Service B has multiple instances, each one talks to Data Manager B Service C reads/writes data from NAS Data Manager A Data Manager B

# Page 22^page=22
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: resiliency patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 30 • Example — circuit breaker in action • How to avoid this problem? • Insert a circuit breaker between B and C Network-Attached Storage (shared file system) Service A calls B to do some work. Service B calls C. Service A uses Data Manager A Service B has multiple instances, each one talks to Data Manager B Service C reads/writes data from NAS Data Manager A Data Manager B Circuit breaker

# Page 23^page=23
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: resiliency patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 31 • Example — circuit breaker in action • Circuit breaker between microservice B and C avoids ripple effect for Applications Service B never invokes C directly B receives an error after timeout Timeout Fast fail Recover seamlessly through periodic retries (half-open circuit) Graceful degradation: Run alternative procedure Circuit breaker wraps and monitors calls to CCircuit breaker call/drop call after time t Happy path Circuit breaker closed Circuit breaker open, hence fallback

# Page 24^page=24
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: security patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 32 • Problem: what about cross-cutting concerns? (e.g., security, logging) • Service (or API) gateway

# Page 25^page=25
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: security patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 33 • Service (or API) gateway • Acts as a mediator. Sits between a service client and a service being invoked • Service clients talk only to the gateway • Gatekeeper for all traffic to microservices → can easily implement authentication/authorization mechanisms Mapping can be either static or dynamic using service discovery and client-side load balancing.

# Page 26^page=26
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: security patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 34 • Service (or API) gateway — is it a single point of failure? • Yes, it can be. • Solution • A Service gateway has multiple instances • A server-side load balancer receives requests and spreads them across available instances

# Page 27^page=27
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: security patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 35 • Authentication/authorization through OAuth2 • Mainstream token-based security protocol (e.g., Facebook, GitHub, …) • Typically implemented or used by a service gateway

# Page 28^page=28
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: security patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 36 • Components of OAuth2 • Protected resource: a resource (in our case, a microservice) you want to protect and ensure that only authenticated users can access • Resource owner: A resource owner defines which applications are allowed to access the microservices. Each application registered by the resource owner has a (name, secret key) pair • Application: application that is going to call the service on a behalf of a user • OAuth2 authentication server: authentication server sits between the application and the services being consumed. The server allows the user to authenticate without having to pass their user credentials to every service the application is going to call

# Page 29^page=29
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: security patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 37 • OAuth2 mechanism • The four components interact together to authenticate the user • The user presents their credentials once to receive a token • Microservices can propagate the token in case of nested calls Authentication server keeps the mapping between resources and authorized applications/users Authentication server (name, secret key) (user, psw) token token valid token? Yes/No Communication mediated by the gateway

# Page 30^page=30
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: communication patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 38 • Synchronous vs asynchronous communication • Why this choice is important • Synchronous communication requires the two communicating parties to be ready to communicate at the same time → tight runtime coupling • Asynchronous communication allows each counterpart to enter in the communication at its own pace

# Page 31^page=31
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: communication patterns • Approach: using an event-driven framework to decouple the two parts SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 39 Service 1 Service 2 • Can support multiple communication styles • Notification: one way, see above • Request/response: two ways • Publish/subscribe: multicast Service 1 Service 2 Service 1 Service 3 Service 4 Service 2

# Page 32^page=32
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: communication patterns SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 45 • Advantages • Loose coupling, higher flexibility, scalability, and availability • Counterparts do not know each other, they just send/receive messages • The set of services sending/receiving messages can change dynamically • If one of the two services is down, the other one can still work through the queue • If a receiver is busy, new replicas can be created to handle the messages stored in a queue • Disadvantages • More complex to develop

# Page 33^page=33
M Camilli, E Di Nitto, M Rossi Microservices: technologies SE2 - SA, Architectural styles 46 • Spring boot • De facto standard framework for developing microservices in Java • https://spring.io/guides/gs/spring-boot/ • Spring Cloud Netflix: • Integration of the following patterns: Service Discovery (Eureka), Circuit Breaker (Hystrix), Intelligent Routing (Zuul) and Client Side Load Balancing (Ribbon) • https://cloud.spring.io/spring-cloud-netflix/reference/html/ • Spring Cloud Stream: • Framework for building event-driven microservices connected with shared messaging systems • Makes use of a variety of “binder implementations” (i.e., frameworks used to exchange messages), e.g., Apache Kafka • https://spring.io/projects/spring-cloud-stream
